title: What time is it?
goal: Tell the time, make plans, and accept one rule that governs every sentence you build from now on: time words stand BEFORE the verb.
bekal: say hours, minutes, and parts of the day correctly
put time words in the right place — and know why they go there

dialogs.title: 對話 — 約時間
dialogs.intro: Budi and Xiaomei want to study together before an exam. They're looking for a time that works.

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.text: [明天|Míngtiān][早上|zǎoshang][有課|yǒu kè]，[下午|xiàwǔ][可以|kěyǐ]。
lines.id: I have class tomorrow morning, but the afternoon works.
lines.literal: tomorrow — morning — have — class, afternoon — can.

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.id: What time in the afternoon is better?

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.text: [兩點半|Liǎng diǎn bàn][我|wǒ][還在|hái zài][上課|shàngkè][耶|ye]。
lines.id: At two thirty I'm still in class.
lines.literal: two — o'clock — half — I — still — (-ing) — go-up-class — (you know).

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.id: Then what time does your class finish?

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.text: [三點|Sān diǎn][十分|shí fēn]。[三點半|Sān diǎn bàn][可以|kěyǐ][嗎|ma]？
lines.literal: three — o'clock — ten — minute. three — o'clock — half — can — (question)?

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.id: Sure. Let's meet at the library.

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.id: OK. What time does the library close?

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.text: [晚上|Wǎnshang][十點|shí diǎn]。[時間|Shíjiān][很多|hěn duō]。
lines.id: Ten at night. Plenty of time.
lines.literal: evening — ten — o'clock. time — very — many.

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.text: [太好了|Tài hǎo le]！[那|Nà][我們|wǒmen][晚上|wǎnshang][一起|yìqǐ][吃飯|chīfàn][吧|ba]。
lines.id: Great! Then let's have dinner together afterwards.
lines.literal: too — good — (now)! then — we — evening — together — eat-rice — (OK).

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.text: [好啊|Hǎo a]！[六點|Liù diǎn][還是|háishì][七點|qī diǎn]？
lines.literal: good — (ah)! six — o'clock — or — seven — o'clock?

lines.speaker: 布迪:
lines.text: [六點|Liù diǎn][吧|ba]，[太晚|tài wǎn][我|wǒ][會|huì][餓|è]。
lines.id: Six, I think — any later and I'll be starving.
lines.literal: six — o'clock — (la), too — late — I — will — hungry.

lines.speaker: 小美:
lines.text: [哈哈|Hāhā]，[好|hǎo]！[明天|Míngtiān][三點半|sān diǎn bàn][見|jiàn]！
lines.id: Haha, OK! See you tomorrow at three thirty!
lines.literal: haha, good! tomorrow — three — o'clock — half — see!

notes: ⚠️ **Two o'clock is 兩點, not 二點.** 點 is a measure word, and before a measure word two is always 兩. It is the only hour that uses 兩; all the others use the ordinary numbers.

**上課 and 下課 are used by teachers and students alike.** 上課 = class is on / go to class; 下課 = class is over. The same 上/下 pattern appears in 上班 (start work) and 下班 (finish work), 上車 (get on a vehicle) and 下車 (get off).
**怎麼樣？ ("how about it?") is the most natural way to suggest something.** *兩點半怎麼樣？* — "How about two thirty?" It's also used to ask for opinions: *這家餐廳怎麼樣？*

**比較 (*bǐjiào*, "comparatively, more") is used far more often than you'd expect.** Taiwanese people use it to soften opinions: *我比較喜歡這個* ("I kind of prefer this one") sounds gentler than stating a choice outright.
⚠️ **太…了 is a complete frame that must not be split.** *太好了！* (great!), *太貴了！* (way too expensive!), *太晚了！* (too late!). Dropping 了 leaves it hanging.

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: Hours use **點** (*diǎn*, literally "dot") and minutes use **分** (*fēn*). The order goes from big to small, like every time expression in Mandarin.

head: Time
中文
Pīnyīn
Note
rows: 三點十五分 / 三點一刻
三點四十五分 / 三點三刻

after: **三點半 means 3:30.** Mandarin counts the half **after** the hour, just like English "half past three" — so 兩點半 is 2:30, never 1:30. (Learners who know German or Dutch "halb drei" should take note.)

**The part of the day always stands IN FRONT of the hour**: 早上八點 (8 a.m.), 下午三點 (3 p.m.), 晚上十點 (10 p.m.). Taiwan uses the twelve-hour clock in conversation; train timetables use the twenty-four-hour clock.

grammars.title: ⚠️ Time goes BEFORE the verb
body: This is the rule English speakers break most often, because English usually puts time at the end: "I'm going tomorrow", "We meet at three thirty".
Mandarin allows only two places, and both are **before the verb**.

head: Sentence
Pīnyīn
Meaning
rows: I get up at seven every day.

after: **With several time words, the order is big to small**: *明天下午三點* (tomorrow afternoon at three) — not *三點下午明天*. This big-to-small rule also applies to dates and addresses, without exception.
⚠️ This rule isn't just about time. **All modifiers** — place (在…), manner (怎麼), company (跟…) — stand before the verb in Mandarin. Once you accept this, half of Mandarin word order is sorted.
One full sentence holding everything: **我明天下午在圖書館跟小美一起念書。** — "Tomorrow afternoon I'm studying with Xiaomei at the library." Time → place → company → verb.

sections.title: Parts of the day and time words

blocks.text: ⚠️ **後天 ("back day") means the day after tomorrow and 前天 ("front day") means the day before yesterday** — the opposite of what English speakers guess, since we think of the future as "ahead". Mandarin pictures time like a queue: what has **already passed** stands in front of you, where you can see it; what hasn't come yet is behind.

head: 中文
Pīnyīn
English
rows: to start work / go to class

blocks.title: A day in Budi's life — and word-order practice
items: **我每天七點起床。** — I get up at seven every day.
**我早上八點上課。** — I go to class at eight in the morning.
**我中午十二點半吃午餐。** — I have lunch at twelve thirty.
**我下午五點回家。** — I go home at five in the afternoon.
**我晚上十一點睡覺。** — I go to bed at eleven at night.
⚠️ Notice that in all five sentences the verb always comes **last**, after every time word.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **A flat no sounds rude; give a reason, then offer another time.** *我今天有事，改天好嗎？* is far more natural than 我不要. This "reason + 改天好嗎" pattern will save you again and again.

items: What time is it now?
